newsitem.title: USA: IBM to shut down World Avenue.
newsitem.headline: IBM to shut down World Avenue.

text.p: International Business Machines Corp. said Tuesday it will close down its virtual shopping mall on the Internet, called World Avenue, as of July 9, due to low traffic.
An IBM spokesman said the computer giant did not want to market to the customers of its customers -- stores with locations at the site -- in order to generate traffic to the shopping site.
"One piece that stood out and that was counter to our strategy was drawing consumers to the site," he said.
"For us to be marketing to their customers was at odds with our strategy," the IBM spokesman said. "It requires a significant ongoing investment."

The mall, which can be found at www.worldavenue.com, currently has three computer stores, two of them IBM's; two department stores, Gottschalks Inc. and Hudson's Bay Co.; eight other speciality stores; and five sports areas selling sporting events tickets and merchandise.

One speciality retailer, Omaha Steaks of Omaha, Neb., said that World Avenue was not a big source of orders, even though the mail-order meat retailer's fastest growing sales arena is from sales at its own Web site and on America Online.
"We like IBM and they like us ... but World Avenue as a source of orders has not been significant," said Todd Simon, a vice president at Omaha Steaks. "I think we get less than 10 orders a week."
Simon said his upfront costs to get on World Avenue were not tremendous.

He said World Avenue needed more marketing to succeed in the crowded Internet space. "I think the key word in online marketing is marketing. ... IBM needed to invest a significant amount of time, money and planning into marketing the site and getting traffic there," Simon added.

Some analysts said they were not surprised at the pending shutdown in light of some of the recent publishing failures on the Web and some earlier retailing debacles, such as MCI Communications Corp.'s MCI Marketplace.

"No one knows how electronic commerce works," said Gary Arlen, president of Arlen Communications Inc. in Bethesda. "It's trying to sell a very complicated business in a world where no one knows how it's supposed to work."
IBM declined to say how much it invested in the site, which it announced last June and launched last autumn. IBM said at the time it received a start-up fee from its vendors.

The start-up fees were estimated at around $30,000 per vendor site. IBM also received a $2,500 monthly maintenance fee to maintain the sites and a 5 percent commission on transactions. IBM said it did not have any specific numbers about site traffic.
"Obviously, it wasn't where we wanted it to be," the spokesman said.

IBM said it will continue to build Web sites, manage them, run them and service them for its customers. "Our role is to serve as the IT (information technology) enabler and partner," the IBM spokesman said. IBM said it still believes that electronic malls can survive on the Internet, if they are marketed by the retailers who know their customers.
For example, IBM is also building an electronic mall for a Hong Kong-based credit card company that will be marketed by Mitsubishi, at http://www.aeonworld.com.
IBM said it has many other successful electronic commerce ventures, such as its development of sites for catalogue retailer L.L. Bean, Borders Books and the Arena di Verona for opera ticket sales.
Separately, IBM unveiled an enhanced version of its VoiceType Simply Speaking dictation software, which allows people to operate a computer with their voice instead of a keyboard and a mouse.
The new software, called Simply Speaking Gold, costs $99. IBM plans to ship the software in Spanish, French, German, Italian, and British English in July.
IBM said its VoiceType Simply Speaking product would now be priced at $49.95.
It also unveiled ViaVoice, a general-purpose continuous-speech dictation product that recognises the spoken word. ViaVoice will be available in August at a price of $199.
